One embodiment provides an apparatus for analyzing body composition and hydration status by detecting the resistance of a human subject at zero and infinite frequencies. The apparatus includes a method for indirectly measuring extracellular water mass, intracellular water mass, lean body mass, and body fat mass; daily changes in extracellular water mass, intracellular water mass, lean body mass, and body fat mass; acute changes in extracellular water mass and intracellular water mass; and individualized calibration of these indirect measurements.

The embodiment further provides a method for fitting mathematical models to serial measurements of indirectly measured lean body mass and fat mass, as well as for dynamic, indirect, individualized measurement—using minimum-variance estimation and prediction—of: daily changes in body composition, defined as changes in glycogen, fat, and protein stores; daily utilized macronutrient energy intake, defined as utilized caloric intake from carbohydrates, fat, and protein; daily macronutrient oxidation rates, defined as the rates of carbohydrate, fat, and protein oxidation; daily resting metabolic rate; daily unknown forms of energy loss or gain; daily rate of endogenous lipolysis; daily nitrogen excretion; daily gluconeogenesis from protein; daily extracellular water mass; daily intracellular water mass; and acute changes in extracellular water mass and intracellular water mass.
outputs.L3:
The apparatus assesses body composition and hydration by measuring the human body’s electrical resistance at both zero and infinite frequencies. These measurements provide the basis for indirectly determining extracellular and intracellular water, lean body mass, and body fat mass, while also detecting both acute and day-to-day changes in these parameters.

To improve accuracy, the method supports individualized calibration of the indirect measurements, accounting for differences in physiology and body composition among users. Mathematical models and minimum-variance estimation techniques are then applied to serial measurements to track and predict changes in glycogen, fat, and protein stores over time.

Using these estimates, the system can calculate a broad range of metabolic and nutritional indicators. These include daily energy intake, macronutrient oxidation, resting metabolic rate, energy gains or losses, lipolysis, nitrogen excretion, and gluconeogenesis. Together, these capabilities provide a detailed, personalized view of changes in hydration, body composition, energy balance, and metabolic activity.
outputs.L4:
The apparatus provides a comprehensive, individualized system for evaluating body composition, hydration, nutritional status, and energy metabolism through measurements of the body’s electrical properties. It applies electrical signals at multiple frequencies and uses the resulting impedance data to estimate human electrical resistance at the theoretical limits of zero frequency and infinite frequency. Because low-frequency current flows primarily through extracellular fluid, while high-frequency current also passes through cell membranes and intracellular fluid, these resistance estimates can be used to distinguish extracellular water from intracellular water and to assess total body water.

The measured electrical data are combined with individualized calibration information, which may include body weight, height, age, sex, geometry, prior measurements, or other physiological and demographic characteristics. Mathematical models relate resistance and impedance to fluid volumes, conductive tissue, and nonconductive tissue. Statistical methods, including minimum-variance estimation, can then integrate current measurements, historical observations, calibration parameters, and model predictions to reduce measurement uncertainty and generate stable estimates for each individual.

From these estimates, the apparatus can determine or infer extracellular water, intracellular water, and total body water, together with changes in fluid distribution over time. The system may further estimate lean body mass, fat mass, body-cell mass, and related body-composition variables. By comparing sequential measurements, it can separate short-term changes caused mainly by hydration from longer-term changes in tissue, thereby improving interpretation of apparent gains or losses in body weight.

The apparatus may also use changes in body composition and fluid compartments to estimate stored energy, nutrient intake, nutrient oxidation, and metabolic activity. Relevant outputs can include changes in fat and lean-tissue energy stores, energy expenditure or balance, and the intake or use of carbohydrate, fat, protein, and other nutrients. These variables can be derived through physiological balance equations and dynamic models that account for the different rates at which water, electrolytes, glycogen, protein, and fat are stored, released, or oxidized.

Measurements can be obtained repeatedly, allowing both daily monitoring and observation of acute physiological changes. Daily measurements may reveal trends in hydration, fat mass, lean mass, and energy balance, while measurements collected over shorter intervals may detect fluid shifts associated with meals, exercise, recovery, illness, environmental exposure, or other interventions. The system can update its individualized parameters as additional data become available, enabling the estimates to adapt to the person rather than relying solely on generalized population equations.

By jointly analyzing electrical resistance, fluid distribution, body composition, and metabolic balance, the apparatus provides a more complete view than a conventional scale or a single-frequency impedance device. Its outputs can support ongoing monitoring of hydration, nutrition, and energy status; help distinguish fluid fluctuations from genuine tissue change; and identify physiological trends that may not be apparent from body weight alone. The resulting information may be presented as current values, changes from baseline, time-series trends, or alerts for significant deviations, providing users or qualified professionals with individualized data for tracking and assessment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe one embodiment of a system for indirectly measuring extracellular water, intracellular water, lean body mass, and body fat, including individualized calibration and minimum-variance prediction from serial measurements.
counterfactuals.output:
One embodiment uses a personalized, multifrequency bioimpedance system combined with an initial reference examination and a serial minimum-variance estimator.

### System components

The system includes:

- A scale or other body-weight sensor;
- Four or more skin electrodes, for example on the wrist and ankle, or segmental electrodes on the hands and feet;
- A current source that applies small alternating currents at multiple frequencies, such as 5 kHz to 1 MHz;
- Voltage-sensing circuitry for determining complex impedance at each frequency;
- A processor storing anthropometric data, calibration coefficients, prior measurements, and uncertainty estimates; and
- Software implementing an electrical body model and a serial state estimator.

### Individualized calibration

During an initial calibration session, the subject undergoes the impedance measurement together with one or more reference measurements. For example:

- Extracellular water, \(ECW\), is measured by bromide or another extracellular tracer;
- Total body water, \(TBW\), is measured by deuterium dilution;
- Intracellular water is calculated as \(ICW=TBW-ECW\); and
- Lean body mass and fat mass are measured by DXA or another reference composition method.

The processor fits a Cole or equivalent electrical model to the multifrequency impedance data to obtain low-frequency resistance \(R_0\), high-frequency resistance \(R_\infty\), characteristic frequency, phase, and optionally segment-specific parameters. Low-frequency current primarily follows extracellular paths, while high-frequency current traverses both extracellular and intracellular compartments.

Subject-specific calibration equations are then determined, for example:

\[
ECW=a_{E,0}+a_{E,1}\frac{L^2}{R_0}+a_{E,2}W+a_{E,3}T
\]

\[
TBW=a_{T,0}+a_{T,1}\frac{L^2}{R_\infty}+a_{T,2}W+a_{T,3}T
\]

where \(L\) is height or conductor length, \(W\) is body weight, and \(T\) can include temperature or another measurement-condition variable. The coefficients may begin with population values and then be updated using the subject’s reference results. ICW is obtained from \(TBW-ECW\), or from a separately calibrated equation.

Lean body mass may be estimated by a personalized relation such as

\[
LBM=b_0+b_1ECW+b_2ICW,
\]

which accounts for the subject’s measured lean-tissue hydration. Fat mass and body-fat percentage are then determined as

\[
FM=W-LBM,\qquad BF\%=100\frac{FM}{W}.
\]

Using DXA calibration permits the processor to fit \(LBM\) or \(FM\) directly when assumptions about constant lean-tissue hydration are undesirable.

### Serial minimum-variance prediction

At each later session, the system records weight and multifrequency impedance under preferably standardized conditions. The resulting instantaneous estimates are combined with prior measurements in a state-space model. A suitable state vector is

\[
x_k=[ECW_k,\ ICW_k,\ LBM_k,\ FM_k,\ \dot{ECW}_k,\ \dot{ICW}_k]^T.
\]

A physiological transition model predicts the current state:

\[
x_{k|k-1}=F_kx_{k-1|k-1},
\]

with process covariance \(Q_k\) representing expected biological change. The new impedance and weight observations satisfy

\[
z_k=H_kx_k+v_k,
\]

where the observation covariance \(R_k\) is individualized from repeated calibration measurements, electrode-contact quality, residual errors, and measurement-condition data.

A Kalman or equivalent best linear unbiased update produces the minimum-variance estimate:

\[
K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^T
(H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k)^{-1},
\]

\[
x_{k|k}=x_{k|k-1}+K_k(z_k-H_kx_{k|k-1}).
\]

Thus a noisy current reading is weighted less heavily, while a precise reading is weighted more heavily. Correlated errors between ECW, ICW, lean mass, fat mass, and serial observations are retained in the covariance matrix rather than treating each estimate independently. Physiological constraints may also be imposed, including nonnegative compartments, \(ECW+ICW=TBW\), and \(LBM+FM=W\).

The system outputs current and predicted ECW, ICW, lean body mass, fat mass, body-fat percentage, changes from baseline, and confidence intervals. Periodic tracer or DXA measurements can update the person-specific coefficients and covariance parameters, allowing calibration to adapt to disease, training, aging, or substantial changes in body composition.

counterfactuals.output: The invention provides a system and method for estimating and forecasting body composition and metabolic substrate dynamics by integrating bioelectrical impedance measurements with a mathematical model of energy and mass balance. Impedance-derived estimates of total body water, extracellular and intracellular water, fat-free mass, fat mass, and related compartments are combined with caloric and macronutrient intake data to model time-varying glycogen, fat, and protein stores. The model applies substrate-specific oxidation rates, basal and activity-dependent metabolic rates, lipolysis and fat-storage kinetics, nitrogen excretion as an indicator of protein catabolism, and gluconeogenesis from amino acids, glycerol, and other precursors. A computational engine reconciles measured impedance changes with predicted fluid shifts and tissue balances, iteratively updating model parameters to distinguish short-term glycogen-associated water variation from longer-term changes in adipose and lean tissue. The resulting estimates may be used to quantify energy expenditure, substrate utilization, and metabolic adaptation, and to generate individualized predictions, alerts, or recommendations relating to nutrition, exercise, weight management, and clinical monitoring.

### Exemplary Patent Claims

1. **A human body composition and hydration monitoring apparatus**, comprising:  
   a plurality of electrodes configured to be electrically coupled to a body of a subject;  
   an excitation circuit configured to apply, through at least a first pair of the plurality of electrodes, electrical excitation signals at a plurality of non-zero frequencies;  
   a measurement circuit configured to measure, through at least a second pair of the plurality of electrodes, electrical responses of the body to the electrical excitation signals;  
   one or more processors; and  
   memory storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the apparatus to:  
   determine, from the electrical responses, complex impedance values corresponding to the plurality of non-zero frequencies;  
   fit a frequency-dependent impedance model to the complex impedance values;  
   determine, using the fitted frequency-dependent impedance model, a zero-frequency resistance representative of extracellular conductive pathways of the body and an infinite-frequency resistance representative of combined intracellular and extracellular conductive pathways of the body;  
   estimate, based at least in part on the zero-frequency resistance and the infinite-frequency resistance, respective amounts of at least two body compartments comprising extracellular fluid and intracellular fluid;  
   store compartment estimates obtained at a plurality of measurement times;  
   determine a daily change in at least one of the body compartments relative to a longitudinal reference;  
   determine an acute change in at least one of the body compartments relative to a short-term reference; and  
   generate an output indicative of at least one of the daily change or the acute change.

2. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the zero-frequency resistance is an extrapolated resistance at a frequency approaching zero and the infinite-frequency resistance is an extrapolated resistance at a frequency approaching infinity.

3. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the frequency-dependent impedance model comprises a Cole model, a Cole-Cole model, an equivalent-circuit model, or a combination thereof.

4. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the instructions cause the apparatus to estimate total body water based on the extracellular fluid and the intracellular fluid.

5. The apparatus of claim 4, wherein the instructions further cause the apparatus to estimate one or more of fat-free mass, fat mass, skeletal muscle mass, body cell mass, or an extracellular-fluid-to-total-body-water ratio.

6. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the longitudinal reference comprises at least one of:  
   a measurement obtained on a preceding day;  
   a moving average of measurements obtained over multiple days;  
   a subject-specific baseline; or  
   a measurement trend predicted from prior measurements.

7. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the short-term reference comprises a measurement obtained within a preceding period of less than twenty-four hours.

8. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the acute change is determined from measurements obtained before and after at least one of fluid ingestion, food ingestion, exercise, sleep, urination, dialysis, administration of a diuretic, intravenous-fluid administration, or a change in posture.

9. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the instructions further cause the apparatus to classify a detected compartment change as an acute hydration change or a longer-term body-composition change based on a magnitude, rate, persistence, or compartment distribution of the detected change.

10. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the instructions further cause the apparatus to distinguish a change predominantly affecting extracellular fluid from a change affecting both extracellular fluid and intracellular fluid by comparing temporal changes in the zero-frequency resistance and the infinite-frequency resistance.

11. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the excitation signals collectively span frequencies on both sides of a characteristic relaxation frequency of body tissue.

12. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the measurement circuit is configured to determine an in-phase component and a quadrature component of each electrical response.

13. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the instructions further cause the apparatus to reject or correct a measurement based on at least one of electrode contact impedance, motion, skin temperature, ambient temperature, body posture, time of day, recent physical activity, or a quality metric associated with fitting the frequency-dependent impedance model.

14. The apparatus of claim 1, further comprising at least one sensor selected from the group consisting of a temperature sensor, motion sensor, posture sensor, weight sensor, optical sensor, and heart-rate sensor, wherein an output of the at least one sensor is used to compensate the compartment estimates or classify the daily change or the acute change.

15. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the plurality of electrodes is incorporated into at least one of a wearable device, scale, handheld device, garment, adhesive patch, bed, seat, or combinations thereof.

16. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the output comprises an alert generated when the daily change or the acute change satisfies a threshold associated with dehydration, fluid overload, edema, recovery from exercise, or a change in lean-tissue mass.

17. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the instructions further cause the apparatus to calculate a confidence value for each compartment estimate based at least in part on residual error between the complex impedance values and the fitted frequency-dependent impedance model.

18. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the daily change is determined using measurements acquired at substantially corresponding times on different days, and the acute change is determined using at least two measurements acquired during a same day.

19. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the instructions further cause the apparatus to update a subject-specific calibration relating the zero-frequency resistance and the infinite-frequency resistance to the respective amounts of the body compartments using one or more of body mass, height, age, sex, limb geometry, or prior compartment estimates.

20. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the output comprises a time-resolved presentation separately identifying:  
   a change in extracellular fluid;  
   a change in intracellular fluid; and  
   a classification of each change as acute, daily, or persistent.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in formal patent terminology, a method for dynamically tracking body composition, fluid status, macronutrient utilization, energy balance, and metabolic processes using calibrated bioimpedance measurements and minimum variance estimation.
counterfactuals.output:
## Patent-Style Description

### Title

**Method and System for Dynamic Estimation of Body Composition, Fluid Distribution, Macronutrient Utilization, Energy Balance, and Metabolic State Using Calibrated Bioimpedance Measurements and Minimum-Variance State Estimation**

### Technical Field

The disclosed subject matter relates generally to physiological monitoring and, more particularly, to computer-implemented methods and systems for dynamically estimating body composition, fluid status, substrate utilization, energy balance, and associated metabolic processes from calibrated bioelectrical impedance measurements, optionally in combination with anthropometric, dietary, activity, environmental, and biochemical measurements.

### Summary of the Disclosure

In one embodiment, a physiological monitoring system repeatedly applies one or more alternating electrical excitation signals to a subject and measures a corresponding complex bioimpedance. The bioimpedance measurements are calibrated to compensate for instrument response, electrode characteristics, anatomical geometry, posture, skin temperature, hydration-independent subject characteristics, and measurement conditions.

A physiological state vector is maintained and recursively updated using a minimum-variance estimator. The state vector may represent total body water, extracellular water, intracellular water, fat-free mass, fat mass, cell mass, glycogen-associated water, gastrointestinal contents, fluid intake and loss, substrate oxidation rates, energy expenditure, energy storage, and other metabolic quantities. A physiological process model predicts temporal evolution of the state vector, and a measurement model relates the predicted state to the calibrated bioimpedance measurements and any auxiliary observations. The estimator combines the prediction and measurements according to their respective uncertainty to produce an updated physiological-state estimate and an associated confidence measure.

### Exemplary Method

A computer-implemented method may comprise:

1. **Acquiring bioimpedance data** by:
   - applying electrical excitation at one or more frequencies to a body or body segment;
   - measuring voltage and current responses through a two-electrode, four-electrode, or multi-electrode arrangement; and
   - determining resistance, reactance, impedance magnitude, phase angle, admittance, or a combination thereof.

2. **Calibrating the bioimpedance data** using one or more calibration parameters derived from:
   - open-circuit, short-circuit, and known-load measurements;
   - electrode-contact impedance;
   - cable and analog-front-end transfer characteristics;
   - subject-specific reference measurements, such as dilution analysis, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, air-displacement plethysmography, magnetic resonance imaging, or indirect calorimetry; and
   - contextual variables including posture, recent exercise, food intake, skin temperature, ambient temperature, time of day, and electrode placement.

3. **Generating impedance-derived features**, including one or more of:
   - zero-frequency or low-frequency resistance;
   - high-frequency resistance;
   - characteristic frequency;
   - extracellular and intracellular resistance;
   - membrane capacitance;
   - Cole-model parameters;
   - segmental impedance ratios;
   - phase-angle trajectories; and
   - temporal derivatives or trends of such quantities.

4. **Defining a physiological state vector**, for example:

\[
\mathbf{x}_k =
\begin{bmatrix}
V_{\mathrm{ECW}} &
V_{\mathrm{ICW}} &
M_{\mathrm{FFM}} &
M_{\mathrm{FM}} &
M_{\mathrm{gly}} &
M_{\mathrm{GI}} &
r_{\mathrm{carb}} &
r_{\mathrm{fat}} &
r_{\mathrm{protein}} &
E_{\mathrm{exp}} &
E_{\mathrm{store}}
\end{bmatrix}^{T},
\]

where \(V_{\mathrm{ECW}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{ICW}}\) denote extracellular and intracellular water volumes, \(M_{\mathrm{FFM}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{FM}}\) denote fat-free and fat mass, \(M_{\mathrm{gly}}\) denotes glycogen mass, \(M_{\mathrm{GI}}\) denotes gastrointestinal content mass, \(r_{\mathrm{carb}}\), \(r_{\mathrm{fat}}\), and \(r_{\mathrm{protein}}\) denote macronutrient utilization or oxidation rates, and \(E_{\mathrm{exp}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{store}}\) denote energy expenditure and stored energy, respectively.

5. **Predicting the physiological state** according to a state-transition model:

\[
\mathbf{x}_{k}^{-}
=
f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}^{+},\mathbf{u}_k,\boldsymbol{\theta})+\mathbf{w}_k,
\]

where \(\mathbf{u}_k\) includes measured or reported inputs, \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) includes subject-specific physiological parameters, and \(\mathbf{w}_k\) represents process uncertainty.

The transition model may enforce water, mass, and energy conservation relationships, including:

\[
\Delta E =
E_{\mathrm{intake}}-E_{\mathrm{expenditure}},
\]

\[
\Delta M =
M_{\mathrm{intake}}-M_{\mathrm{excretion}}-M_{\mathrm{oxidation}},
\]

and compartmental fluid-transfer relationships among plasma, interstitial, and intracellular spaces.

6. **Forming a measurement vector** comprising calibrated bioimpedance features and, optionally, body mass, heart rate, activity, respiratory gas measurements, dietary intake, urine output, temperature, glucose, ketones, or other sensor data:

\[
\mathbf{z}_k=h(\mathbf{x}_k,\boldsymbol{\theta})+\mathbf{v}_k,
\]

where \(h(\cdot)\) is a measurement model and \(\mathbf{v}_k\) represents measurement uncertainty.

7. **Recursively updating the physiological state** using a minimum-variance estimator, such as a Kalman filter, extended Kalman filter, unscented Kalman filter, ensemble Kalman filter, information filter, or constrained Bayesian estimator.

For a linearized implementation, the update may comprise:

\[
\mathbf{K}_k =
\mathbf{P}_{k}^{-}\mathbf{H}_{k}^{T}
\left(
\mathbf{H}_{k}\mathbf{P}_{k}^{-}\mathbf{H}_{k}^{T}
+\mathbf{R}_{k}
\right)^{-1},
\]

\[
\mathbf{x}_{k}^{+}
=
\mathbf{x}_{k}^{-}
+
\mathbf{K}_k
\left[
\mathbf{z}_k-h(\mathbf{x}_{k}^{-})
\right],
\]

\[
\mathbf{P}_{k}^{+}
=
(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_{k}^{-},
\]

where \(\mathbf{P}_{k}^{-}\) and \(\mathbf{P}_{k}^{+}\) are prior and posterior state-error covariance matrices, \(\mathbf{R}_k\) is a measurement-noise covariance matrix, and \(\mathbf{K}_k\) is a gain selected to minimize posterior estimation-error variance.

8. **Applying physiological constraints**, including non-negativity, permissible compartment ranges, conservation of total mass, bounded rates of tissue change, osmotic relationships, and consistency between energy storage and estimated tissue change.

9. **Producing dynamic outputs** indicative of:
   - total, extracellular, and intracellular body water;
   - fluid retention, dehydration, or compartmental fluid shifts;
   - fat mass, fat-free mass, and active cell mass;
   - glycogen depletion or repletion;
   - carbohydrate, lipid, and protein utilization;
   - resting and activity-related energy expenditure;
   - net energy balance;
   - rates of anabolic or catabolic change; and
   - uncertainty, confidence intervals, or data-quality indicators associated with each output.

### Adaptive Operation

The process-noise and measurement-noise covariance matrices may be adjusted in response to signal quality, electrode-contact stability, detected motion, deviation from a habitual measurement posture, elapsed time since food or fluid intake, or the magnitude of a measurement innovation. Measurements determined to be corrupted may be down-weighted or rejected. If data are unavailable, the estimator may continue to propagate the physiological state using the process model while increasing the corresponding uncertainty.

Subject-specific parameters may be updated over time by comparing estimated states with reference observations. Such adaptation may account for differences in body geometry, tissue resistivity, age, sex, ethnicity, training status, disease state, or medication use.

### Exemplary Independent Claim Format

**A computer-implemented method for dynamically estimating a physiological condition of a subject, the method comprising:**

- obtaining, at a plurality of measurement times, complex bioelectrical impedance data generated by applying electrical excitation at a plurality of frequencies to at least one anatomical region of the subject;
- calibrating the complex bioelectrical impedance data according to at least one instrument calibration parameter and at least one subject-specific or measurement-context parameter;
- determining, from the calibrated data, a plurality of impedance features representative of conductive fluid volume and cellular tissue properties;
- maintaining a state vector representing at least body-fluid compartments, body-composition compartments, macronutrient utilization, and energy balance;
- predicting the state vector according to a physiological state-transition model incorporating at least one mass-balance, fluid-balance, or energy-balance relationship;
- determining an innovation between the calibrated impedance features and predicted impedance features generated by a measurement model;
- updating the state vector using a minimum-variance estimator that weights the innovation according to process uncertainty and measurement uncertainty; and
- generating an output indicative of at least one of body composition, fluid status, macronutrient utilization, energy expenditure, energy storage, or metabolic change.

Bioimpedance principally provides information concerning conductive fluid distribution and tissue electrical properties. Accordingly, estimates of substrate utilization and metabolic flux are preferably generated through model-based fusion with energy-balance constraints or auxiliary measurements, rather than being treated as direct measurements of macronutrient oxidation.
